then.text: A whole mill of hands, and not one of them a tea towel. Thank you, {player}. It looks like it was always going to be here.
Mervyn has been round three times to check the rivets are straight. There are no rivets. He checks anyway.

else.text: Sunlight through high windows. Bolts of linen on one table, a ship's rivet bucket on another, a stone from the Wall on the third. The air smells of oil and wet wool.
That's it, {player}. The heater boys, the doffers and the wallers. Three trades with their own names on the wall. It's not much, and it's everything.
A mill that's open is a mill that gets looked after. The Council has stopped talking about the bulldozer, and the kettle has stopped being the most important thing in the building.
Take this. It's a tally. Hold it up in any Ulster shop and they'll know you for one of ours.
And one more. A flaxling was living in the old dye shed. It's been following me around for weeks. I think it prefers you.

arcni_mill_loom.text: That loom's from before my time, and it still works. I demonstrate on Saturdays. The first thing they ask is how I stood the noise. The answer's I didn't. I just got used to it.
Plain linen. Damask is fancier: that's the pattern woven in. I wove a lot of tablecloths in my day and never once saw one on a table I could afford.

arcni_mill_wall.text: They gave me a corner of the hall for a stretch of dry-stone to show visitors. A wall on a floor. It feels like a fish in a bath, but folk like it.
Come the summer, I'll teach the young lads to put a throughstone in. If the sheep can do without it, so can they. No: they can't.
